label: E8
title: Organs and systems that matter for metabolism

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Absorbed material leaves the gut by two different routes. Water-soluble nutrients enter the capillary blood (the smallest blood vessels) in the villi, the tiny fingers lining the gut, and travel to the liver via the hepatic portal vein. Lipid-soluble nutrients diffuse through the plasma membrane, are packaged inside the cell, and enter the lacteals, the lymph vessels of the villi. Lymphatic vessels then carry them to the general circulation, the blood that goes round the whole body.

The liver is the largest gland in the body. Besides its role in digestion it has many roles in metabolism and regulation. Under the hepatic portal circulation, all blood from the alimentary canal (the gut tube) passes through the liver. Drugs and toxins are absorbed along with the nutrients. After processing what the blood brings, the liver releases the nutrients other cells need back into the blood. It stores excess glucose as glycogen and converts glycogen back into glucose.

The liver’s digestive role is to produce bile and export it to the small intestine. The gallbladder stores, concentrates and releases that bile.

The pancreas has two separate functions. As an exocrine gland it produces pancreatic juice, containing digestive enzymes and bicarbonate ions, and delivers it to the small intestine through a duct. As an endocrine gland it secretes hormones directly into the surrounding fluid. Its pancreatic islets, formerly known as the islets of Langerhans, secrete glucagon, insulin, somatostatin and pancreatic polypeptide. The alpha cell produces glucagon and the beta cell produces insulin. Receptors located in the pancreas sense blood glucose levels, and the pancreatic cells secrete glucagon or insulin accordingly.

An endocrine organ secretes a chemical, the hormone, into the extracellular fluid, the fluid around its own cells. From there the blood vessels transport hormones throughout the body. A hormone binds to receptors on target cells, inducing a characteristic response. Adipose tissue is among the tissues known to produce hormones.

Elevated blood glucose stimulates the release of insulin. The primary function of insulin is to facilitate the uptake of glucose into body cells. Insulin also stimulates the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen for storage, and promotes triglyceride and protein synthesis. Skeletal muscle cells and adipose cells are the primary targets of insulin.

Low blood glucose stimulates the release of glucagon. Glucagon stimulates the liver to convert its stores of glycogen back into glucose, which is released into the circulation. It stimulates the liver to take up amino acids from the blood and convert them into glucose. It also stimulates lipolysis, the breakdown of stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol.

Nothing stated here fixes how much of anything any of these organs handles.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
The section on the cell and the section on metabolism gave you a cell, and then the chemistry that goes on inside it. This one is about which parts of a body do which part of that work.

Six of them matter here. The gut, the liver, the pancreas, fat tissue, muscle and the brain.

The gut is a tube. Its proper name is the alimentary canal.

Until a molecule passes through the wall of the tube and into your blood, your body can do nothing with it.

So the gut has one job. Cut food down until the pieces are small enough to go through the wall, and then let them through. It is covered in tiny fingers, called villi, and the pieces cross into the vessels inside those fingers.

What dissolves in water and what dissolves in fat leave the gut by two different roads.

Whatever dissolves in water goes into the smallest blood vessels there, the capillaries. That blood runs straight to the liver, along a vein called the hepatic portal vein.

Whatever dissolves in fat goes into a different set of vessels, the lymph vessels. In the villi they are called lacteals. They empty into the blood further along, past the liver, into the general circulation, the blood that goes round the whole body. So fat reaches the rest of the body before the liver has looked at it, and sugar does not.

Now the liver.

Every drop of blood leaving the gut goes through the liver before it goes anywhere else. All of it. This route is called the hepatic portal circulation.

It sits in the doorway.

It also holds part of the small store. Sugar that nobody needs this minute is packed away there as glycogen, which you met in the section on metabolism.

And it makes bile, which it sends down into the gut, where it breaks large blobs of fat into tiny ones.

Next to the liver is a small bag called the gallbladder. It holds bile, concentrates it and lets it out.

Now the pancreas, and it does two completely separate jobs. Keep them apart in your head, or every sentence you ever read about the pancreas will confuse you.

The pancreas makes a juice full of enzymes and sends it down a tube into the gut, where the juice helps take food apart.

Scattered through the pancreas are small islands of another kind of cell, called islets. They put chemicals straight into the blood, and two of those chemicals run the rest of this section.

A chemical made in one part of the body that affects other parts some distance away is called a hormone.

A hormone starts in a gland, which is an organ whose job is to make it. The gland lets it out into the fluid around its own cells, called the extracellular fluid. From there the blood carries it on, and the blood goes everywhere.

A hormone does not travel to a destination. It goes everywhere, past everything.

It washes past every cell in the body. It does something only where there is a receptor shaped to hold it.

Two things follow, and both matter.

First, if you want to know where a hormone acts, never ask where it went. Ask which cells carry the receptor.

Second, the same hormone can do different things in different places. What happens next depends on the cell it landed in, not on the hormone. So “this hormone does that” is an unfinished sentence until it names a tissue.

Eat, and sugar crosses the gut wall into the blood.

The islets notice. Blood sugar, meaning the glucose in the blood, is high, and one kind of cell in them, called a beta cell, releases insulin.

Insulin’s main job is to move glucose out of the blood and into cells. It lands on a receptor. The cell responds by bringing glucose-carrying proteins to its own surface, where they can take glucose in.

Muscle cells and fat cells are the ones insulin acts on most.

Blood sugar falls.

The same islets notice that too. A different cell in them, called an alpha cell, releases a different hormone. Its name is glucagon.

Glucagon runs the other way, and mostly at the liver. It tells the liver to turn its glycogen back into glucose and push that glucose out into the blood. It tells the liver to build new glucose out of amino acids.

Sugar up, insulin, stores fill. Sugar down, glucagon, stores empty.

Neither half is the good half. A store that only ever filled would not be a store.

Glucose is the fuel every cell prefers. But some organs can use nothing else, and the brain is the one that matters. So blood sugar must not be allowed to fall too far. That is what glucagon is there for.

The brain does not need insulin to take glucose in. Neither do red blood cells, the liver, the kidneys or the lining of the gut. They take glucose out of the blood whether insulin is there or not.

Muscle and fat wait for insulin. The brain does not wait.

Adipose tissue, the large store from the section on metabolism, makes hormones of its own and puts them into the blood. That makes it an organ of the same kind as the pancreas.

Muscle is the other tissue insulin acts on most. It is a store too, and it holds glycogen, as the liver does.

All of it is what each part does. None of it is how much.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
The rule is this. Insulin is what lets sugar into cells.

The brain runs on sugar. So the brain should be the first thing to fail, and it should fail for want of a way in.

Now go and check it.

Open OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, section 17.9, The Endocrine Pancreas, at https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/17-9-the-endocrine-pancreas. Open your browser’s find box. Search inside the page for insulin receptors.

Red blood cells, as well as cells of the brain, liver, kidneys, and the lining of the small intestine, do not have insulin receptors on their cell membranes and do not require insulin for glucose uptake.

The brain is on it. So is the liver.

Read to the end of the sentence: “do not require insulin for glucose uptake”. That is the half to keep. The same page says insulin makes the liver store glycogen, so the liver is not deaf to insulin. What it does not need insulin for is taking glucose in.

The rule is right about some cells and silent about others, and nobody told you which were which.

Search the same page for primary targets.

…skeletal muscle cells and adipose cells are the primary targets of insulin.

Muscle and fat wait for insulin. The brain does not wait at all.

Open section 24.2, Carbohydrate Metabolism, at https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/24-2-carbohydrate-metabolism, and search for only glucose.

Certain key organs, including the brain, can use only glucose as an energy source; therefore, it is essential that the body maintain a minimum blood glucose concentration.

The brain can burn nothing but glucose. It takes glucose out of the blood whether or not insulin is there. So nothing protects the brain when blood sugar runs low except putting more sugar into the blood.

And that is why there are two hormones and not one. One to put sugar away when there is plenty. One to get it back out when there is not.

Here are the two, side by side.

hormone released when blood sugar is made by what it does to the stores
insulin high beta cells fills them
glucagon low alpha cells empties them

Take a person who eats a meal at one o’clock and does not eat again until eight. Follow the seven hours.

One o’clock. Sugar goes into the blood, and the blood carrying it runs first to the liver.

Blood sugar rises. Beta cells release insulin, and the insulin goes everywhere in the blood.

Muscle cells and fat cells bring glucose carriers to their surface and take sugar in. The liver packs spare sugar away as glycogen.

Four o’clock. The brain has not stopped, and neither has anything else, so blood sugar starts to fall.

Alpha cells release glucagon.

The liver turns its glycogen back into glucose and pushes it out into the blood. It also starts building new glucose out of amino acids.

Eight o’clock. Blood sugar is still in a workable range and the brain has never gone short.

The store filling and the store emptying are both the mechanism working. Neither one is a failure, and neither one is a success.

Everything absorbed from the gut in water goes through the liver before the rest of the body sees it. All of it. So whenever somebody tells you that a substance taken by mouth does what that substance does when it is injected, you have one question ready.

What did the liver do to it first?

The answer is often that nobody checked.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
Six organs is a working list and not the whole body.

The table gives no amount, no speed and no threshold at which anything happens.

Insulin and glucagon are not the only hormones the islands make, and they are not the only hormones acting on these stores.

The brain or the liver not needing insulin does not mean it is untouched by insulin. What the source establishes is narrower: it takes glucose without it.

The two roads out of the gut describe a route and nothing else.

The seven hours are a shape, not a measurement. The order of events is what the sources carry.

Any question whose answer is a number is outside this section.

What changes when part of the loop stops working is a later subject, and nothing here settles it.

points.html: “Insulin is what lets sugar into cells” is wrong for several of the cells that matter most. The brain, the liver, the kidneys, red blood cells and the lining of the gut do not need insulin to take glucose in. So make any claim about insulin name its tissue, and say whether it is about uptake or about something else.
A hormone does not travel to a target. It goes everywhere in the blood and acts where a receptor holds it. Ask which cells carry the receptor, and what those cells do when it binds.
So “this hormone causes that” is unfinished until it names a tissue. Ask for the tissue before you accept the claim.
Everything taken up from the gut in water passes through the liver before the rest of the body sees it. All of it, every time.

A store filling and a store emptying are both the mechanism working. Insulin fills, glucagon empties, and both run in the same person every day. So when weight comes back after it fell, say what the section has given you. A store fills under one signal and empties under another, and that loop runs the same way in every person. This section does not tell you which signals, or by how much. And it never licenses a sentence about the person’s character.
Adipose tissue makes hormones of its own and puts them into the blood. That makes it an organ with a job, not a bag that things end up in.

The pancreas does two separate jobs and a trainee who merges them misreads every pancreas sentence after that. One job sends a juice full of enzymes down a tube into the gut. The other puts hormones straight into the blood.
Nothing here carries an organ’s share of energy use, a concentration in blood, or a rate. Refuse any argument that uses it that way.

blocks.prompt:
Without looking back, name the six organs or tissues this section covers. Write one line for each, saying what it does with energy.

Then say what a hormone is, and how it gets to the place where it acts.
blocks.answer:
The six are the gut, the liver, the pancreas, adipose tissue, muscle and the brain.

The gut cuts food into pieces small enough to cross its wall, and lets them through into the blood. What dissolves in water goes from there to the liver. What dissolves in fat takes another road and joins the blood further along.

The liver takes all the blood coming from the gut before anything else does. It works on what arrives and passes on what the body needs. It stores spare sugar as glycogen and turns glycogen back into sugar. It also makes bile, which breaks large blobs of fat into tiny ones.

The pancreas does two jobs. It sends a juice full of enzymes down a tube into the gut. And small islands inside it put insulin and glucagon straight into the blood.

Adipose tissue holds triglyceride until it is needed. It is one of the two tissues insulin acts on most, and it makes hormones of its own.

Muscle is the other tissue insulin acts on most, and it holds glycogen.

The brain runs on glucose and can use nothing else. It takes glucose from the blood without needing insulin.

Now the hormone. A hormone is a chemical that a gland puts into the fluid around its own cells. That fluid drains into the blood, and the blood carries it all over the body.

How it gets where it acts: it does not go anywhere in particular. It goes everywhere. It acts only where a cell carries a receptor shaped to hold it. When it binds, the receptor changes shape, and something happens inside that cell.

One check on your own answer. If you wrote that a hormone travels to its target organ, go back. That picture will make every later sentence about side effects come out wrong.

blocks.prompt:
A patient information leaflet contains this paragraph.

Fat cells are simply storage bags. Once they are full, the body has nowhere left to put the extra energy, and that is when the problems start. The answer is to stop filling them.

The leaflet is made up for this exercise. Say what is wrong with it, sentence by sentence, and say what you would put in its place.
blocks.answer:
Three sentences, and each one is wrong in a different way.

The first sentence is wrong as biology. Adipose tissue is not a bag. It makes hormones of its own and puts them into the blood, which makes it an organ that signals to the rest of the body. The word “simply” is doing the damage, and it is doing it in a leaflet a patient will read.

The second sentence is a claim with a number hidden in it. “Once they are full” asserts a capacity. Nothing in this section gives you one. No figure in the book behind this section would survive a check either, because every figure in it is stated with no study named. A quantity asserted without a measurement is the kind of sentence that sounds like physiology and is not.

It is also wrong about the loop. This section gives you a store that fills and a store that empties, several times a day, under two hormones that run opposite ways. The leaflet describes a one-way process. A store that only ever filled would not be a store.

The third sentence takes a mechanism and turns it into an instruction for the reader. That is a separate move and it needs its own evidence, which the leaflet does not offer.

What to put in its place. Say what adipose tissue does, in the same voice you would use for the liver. It holds triglyceride until it is needed. It releases it under a signal. It also makes hormones, which is why it counts as an organ rather than a place.

And take out the word “simply”, wherever it appears. Nothing in this section is simple, and the word is only ever doing work on the reader rather than on the subject.

blocks.prompt:
A first-year resident has ten minutes and a whiteboard. They have just told a patient that insulin is the key that unlocks the cell and lets sugar in.

Teach them insulin and glucagon so that they never say a sentence about insulin again without naming a tissue.
blocks.answer:
Ten minutes and a whiteboard, and the sentence they used is the one everybody is taught. Say that first, because it is true and it stops them defending it.

Draw a line across the board and mark two ends. Write “sugar high” at one end and “sugar low” at the other. Nothing else yet.

Ask them what the pancreas does at each end. They will get insulin and glucagon in the right places. Write the two names under the two ends.

Now add one row under each: what it does to the stores. Insulin fills them. Glucagon empties them. Let them see that the picture is a loop and not a rule.

Now break their sentence, and do it by asking rather than telling. Ask which organ runs on glucose and can use nothing else. They will say the brain. Ask whether the brain needs insulin to take glucose in.

Let them answer, then give them the sentence from the book. The brain, the liver, the kidneys, red blood cells and the lining of the gut need no insulin to take glucose in. The liver still answers to insulin in other ways: insulin makes it store glycogen.

Now go back to the board and write the two tissues that do wait for insulin: muscle and fat.

Then ask the question that fixes the habit. If the brain needs no insulin, what was the key unlocking? They will see it. The key picture had one door in it. There are at least two kinds of cell, and only one of them needs the key to let sugar in.

Close with the rule you want them using tomorrow. Any sentence about a hormone names a tissue. Not “insulin lets sugar into cells”, but “insulin brings glucose carriers to the surface of muscle and fat cells”.

And tell them why it matters to the patient and not only to the exam. A patient who is told that insulin lets sugar into cells will conclude that without it the brain starves for want of a way in. That is not what happens, and a patient acting on it will do the wrong thing.
